sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Everything in Part 7 so far — slash commands, hooks, permissions, Plan Mode — makes a single Claude Code session more capable. This lesson is about something different: how to keep a *feature* coherent across many sessions, days, or even team members, when no single conversation holds the whole picture. The answer that's emerged across the industry in 2025–2026 is spec-driven development (SDD): write the requirements down as a real file before you start, implement against it, and review the result against what you wrote — not against your memory of what you meant.

## Vibe Coding vs. Spec-Driven Development

**Vibe coding** is the default mode most people fall into with any AI coding tool: you describe what you want in a prompt, the agent produces something, you look at it, you say "no, more like this" or "yes, but also handle X," and you iterate by feel until it seems right. There's no artifact describing what "done" means — just a conversation and your evolving intuition.

This works well for small, contained tasks. It breaks down for two related reasons as tasks grow:

**Intent drift** — over a long session (or across several sessions), the requirement quietly mutates. You asked for a login form with email/password; ten prompts later you're debugging OAuth edge cases nobody asked for, because each incremental request made sense on its own but the sum has wandered from the original goal.

**Context decay** — Claude Code's context window is large but not infinite, and compaction (lesson 7-13's Memory hook pattern exists specifically to fight this) means details from early in a long session can get summarized away or dropped by the time you're deep into implementation. A vibe-coded session has no external anchor to check against when this happens — the only record of what you originally wanted lives in a conversation that's partially decayed.

**Spec-driven development** addresses both by moving the requirement out of the conversation and into a persistent file: a spec (or `SPEC.md`, or a `specs/` folder) that states the problem, the requirements, and what "done" looks like, *before* implementation starts. The agent implements against that file. You review the diff against that file. If context gets compacted or you resume three days later, the spec is still there, unchanged, saying exactly what you agreed to build.

## Real Tools Doing This in 2025-2026

This isn't a theoretical pattern — it's been formalized by multiple serious players:

**GitHub Spec Kit** — An open-source toolkit and workflow from GitHub for spec-driven AI development: you author a structured specification, generate an implementation plan from it, and have an AI agent build against that plan, with the spec remaining the source of truth throughout.

**AWS Kiro** — An AI IDE built around the same core idea: instead of jumping straight to code generation, Kiro has you (and the agent, collaboratively) produce requirements and a design document first, then generates an implementation task list from those artifacts, and tracks progress against them.

**The "Agent OS" pattern** — A broader convention, not a single product: teams maintain a living set of spec files alongside the codebase itself (often versioned in the same repo), so the specs are never a separate Confluence page that drifts out of sync — they're checked in, reviewed in the same pull request as the code, and updated when requirements change instead of silently going stale.

The common thread across all three: the spec is a first-class, persistent artifact — not a paragraph typed into a chat box and then lost to scrollback.

## The Natural Extension of Plan Mode

You already have the raw material for this from lesson 7-10. Plan Mode (Shift+Tab) makes Claude propose a plan and pause before executing — you review the plan, then approve or reject it. That's SDD's core discipline (review intent before implementation) already built into Claude Code.

The limitation of Plan Mode alone: the plan is *ephemeral*. It exists for that one exchange, in that one session. Once you approve it and Claude starts working, the plan itself isn't saved anywhere you'd naturally look again — if the session gets compacted, or you close the terminal and come back tomorrow, the plan is gone and only the resulting code remains as evidence of what was intended.

Spec-driven development is Plan Mode's plan, promoted to a permanent file:

1. Instead of asking Claude to plan in the moment, you (optionally with Claude's help) write a `SPEC.md` or `specs/feature-name.md` file first.
2. That file is committed to the repo, just like code — it can be reviewed in a pull request before a single line of implementation exists.
3. You point Claude Code at the spec file and ask it to implement against it — the equivalent of Plan Mode's "here's what I'm about to do," except now durable and re-readable at any point, by you, a teammate, or Claude itself after a context reset.
4. When the implementation is done, you review the diff against the spec, not against your memory of the conversation — closing the loop that a vibe-coded session never explicitly closes.

Plan Mode is the right tool inside a single session for a change too risky to let rip unreviewed. SDD is the right tool when the *session itself* isn't the unit that needs to hold together — the feature is.

## When SDD Is Worth the Overhead — and When It Isn't

Writing a spec is not free — it costs time up front and adds a file to maintain. Use it deliberately, not by default.

**SDD is worth it when:**
- The feature will span multiple sessions (today's context won't be tomorrow's context — you need an anchor that survives the gap)
- Someone else will pick up the work, or review it, without having been in the original conversation — a teammate, a future you, or a code reviewer
- The cost of building the wrong thing is high — a customer-facing feature, a migration, anything expensive to redo
- You've noticed "wait, what were we even building?" happen on a task before — that's a direct signal the next similar task needs a spec

**Vibe coding is fine when:**
- The output is throwaway — a one-off script, a data-munging task you'll never look at again
- You're exploring solo and don't yet know what you want — writing a spec for a problem you haven't finished defining just produces a spec you'll rewrite anyway
- The task is small enough to hold entirely in your head and finish in one sitting
- You're prototyping to *discover* the requirements, not implementing requirements you already have

A useful heuristic: if you'd be uncomfortable handing the task to a new Claude Code session with zero conversation history and just the spec file, you don't have a spec yet — you have a vibe with extra steps.

## Worked Example: Spec → Implementation → Review

Suppose you want to add rate limiting to an internal API endpoint. Here's the SDD version end to end.

**1. Write the spec** (`specs/rate-limiting.md`):

```markdown
# Spec: Rate Limiting for /api/reports

## Problem
The /api/reports endpoint has no rate limit. A single misbehaving
client script recently sent 400 requests/second and degraded the
service for everyone else.

## Requirements
- Limit each API key to 60 requests per minute on /api/reports
- Return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when exceeded
- Limit is per API key, not global
- Must not add more than 5ms of latency per request

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] 61st request within 60 seconds from the same key returns 429
- [ ] Retry-After header value is accurate to within 1 second
- [ ] A different API key is unaffected by another key's rate limit
- [ ] Existing endpoint tests still pass

## Out of Scope
- Rate limiting other endpoints (follow-up work)
- A configurable per-customer limit (hardcode 60/min for now)
```

**2. Implement against it.** Point Claude Code at the file: *"Implement `specs/rate-limiting.md`. Ask me anything that's ambiguous before you start."* Claude Code may reasonably ask which rate-limiting library or storage backend to use (Redis? in-memory?) if the spec doesn't say — that's the spec doing its job by surfacing a gap before code gets written, not after.

**3. Review the diff against the spec, not against vibes.** Go through the acceptance criteria checklist item by item against the actual diff: does a 61st request really return 429? Is the Retry-After header actually accurate? Did the implementation quietly rate-limit globally instead of per-key (a common shortcut an agent might take)? This is a materially different review than "does this look reasonable" — you're checking a specific, written contract, which is exactly what makes the review catch things a vibe-check would miss.

**Keep specs small and scoped to one feature.** A `specs/` folder with one file per feature (rate-limiting.md, csv-export.md, sso-login.md) ages much better than one giant `SPEC.md` that tries to describe the whole product — small specs stay accurate because they're cheap to update, and a stale spec is worse than no spec because it actively misleads the next person (or agent) who reads it.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Write a Spec and Implement It Against Claude Code
sections.content:
You will write a real one-page spec for a real small feature or change you actually want in one of your own projects, then have Claude Code implement it against that spec. This produces a shipped (or shippable) change plus a reusable spec file — not a toy exercise.

**Step 1 — Pick a real, small feature** you genuinely want in a project you own: a new CLI flag, a validation rule, an export format, a small UI addition — something finishable in under an hour of agent work.

**Step 2 — Write the spec** as a markdown file (`specs/<feature-name>.md` in the project, or a scratch file if you'd rather not commit the folder structure yet) with these four sections, following the worked example above:
- **Problem** — what's wrong or missing today, in 1-3 sentences
- **Requirements** — the specific, testable things the feature must do
- **Acceptance Criteria** — a checklist you could tick off by hand
- **Out of Scope** — what you're deliberately NOT building right now, so neither you nor Claude scope-creeps into it

**Step 3 — Hand it to Claude Code:** open the project and say *"Implement `specs/<feature-name>.md`. If anything is ambiguous, ask me before you start rather than guessing."*

**Step 4 — Let Claude ask its clarifying questions** (if any) and answer them — then let it implement.

**Step 5 — Review the diff against the acceptance criteria checklist**, item by item, not against your general impression. Tick off each one only after verifying it against the actual code (run it, don't just read it, wherever practical).

**Step 6 — Fix or flag any acceptance criterion that doesn't actually pass**, then commit the change together with the spec file.

**Outcome:** a real feature shipped in one of your own projects, a spec file that documents why it exists and what it was supposed to do, and a review you can defend criterion-by-criterion rather than "looks fine to me."

sections.question: A team's feature has been in progress across four separate Claude Code sessions over two weeks, with two different engineers picking it up at different points. On the third session, the engineer notices the implementation has drifted from what was originally discussed in session one — which no one has full context on anymore. What would have prevented this most directly?
options: Using Plan Mode (Shift+Tab) in every single session to review the plan before each change

Writing a persistent spec file at the start (SPEC.md or specs/feature.md) that survives across sessions and engineers, so every session and every engineer implements and reviews against the same written requirements instead of a scattered memory of session one's conversation
Asking Claude Code to summarize the previous session's conversation at the start of each new session
Assigning the whole feature to one engineer so context isn't split across people
sections.explanation: This is exactly the scenario SDD is built for: multi-session work with a handoff between people, where no single conversation (or single person's memory) holds the whole picture. Plan Mode (A) helps within a session but its plan is ephemeral — it doesn't survive to session four or transfer to a different engineer. Summarizing the previous session (C) is better than nothing but is still a lossy, informal substitute for a written spec, and drift can creep into the summary itself. Assigning one engineer (D) avoids the handoff problem but doesn't solve context decay across two weeks and four sessions for that one person either — and isn't always realistic given real team constraints.

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Write Your Personal Spec-First vs. Vibe-Coding Rule
sections.content:
Not every task deserves a spec, and treating every change as spec-worthy would slow you down for no benefit. This workshop produces a written personal rule you'll actually consult before starting your next Claude Code task.

**Step 1 — Look back at your last 2-3 weeks of Claude Code use** (or, if you're new to it, think through your typical work). List a few tasks that went smoothly with vibe coding, and — if any come to mind — a task where you lost track of what you were originally building partway through.

**Step 2 — Draft your personal rule**, answering concretely:
- What size or type of task do you default to vibe coding for? (e.g., anything under ~30 minutes, solo exploration, throwaway scripts)
- What triggers you to stop and write a spec instead? (e.g., anything spanning more than one session, anything a teammate will review or continue, anything customer-facing)
- Where will your specs live? (a `specs/` folder committed to the repo, a personal scratch folder, a Claude Project)
- What's your minimum spec format — do you always use the four sections from this lesson (Problem / Requirements / Acceptance Criteria / Out of Scope), or a lighter version for smaller tasks?

**Step 3 — Ask Claude Code (or Claude.ai):** *"Here's my personal rule for when I use spec-driven development vs. vibe coding: [paste your Step 2 answers]. What edge case in my own workflow does this rule not clearly cover?"* Adjust based on what it surfaces.

**Step 4 — Save the finished rule** as a real file — `docs/how-i-work.md`, a note in your Claude Code CLAUDE.md, or a personal notes doc — somewhere you'll actually see it again, not a one-off answer you'll forget.

**Outcome:** a concrete, written decision rule — not a vague intention to "be more disciplined" — that you can apply the next time you sit down to start a Claude Code task.

sections.question: A solo developer is spending an evening exploring three different approaches to a data visualization idea, throwing away two of them, with no teammates involved and no plan to keep any of the code beyond tonight. Based on this lesson's guidance, what's the right approach?
options: Write a full spec (Problem/Requirements/Acceptance Criteria/Out of Scope) for each of the three approaches before trying any of them

Vibe code all three — this is solo exploratory work where the requirements aren't even known yet, which is precisely the case where a spec would just be rewritten as understanding develops, with no handoff or multi-session risk to justify the overhead
Use GitHub Spec Kit to formalize the exploration since it's the industry-standard tool
Skip Claude Code entirely for exploratory work since spec-driven development is the only correct way to use AI coding agents
sections.explanation: This is squarely in the 'vibe coding is fine' category from this lesson: solo, exploratory, throwaway, single-sitting, and the requirements aren't even settled yet — writing a spec before you know what you're building just produces a spec you'll immediately discard or rewrite. SDD earns its overhead from multi-session persistence, handoffs, and high cost-of-being-wrong — none of which apply here. Option D overstates the lesson — SDD and vibe coding are both legitimate tools for different situations, not a strict hierarchy where one is 'the only correct way.'

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 7-14 — and Part 7.** You can now distinguish vibe coding from spec-driven development, and you know why the latter exists: to survive intent drift and context decay across sessions that a single conversation (even with Plan Mode) can't guarantee on its own. You know the real tools formalizing this pattern — GitHub Spec Kit, AWS Kiro, and the Agent OS convention of living spec files in the repo. You've written a real spec, implemented it with Claude Code, and reviewed the diff against acceptance criteria rather than vibes — and you've set your own rule for when that overhead is worth paying. Part 20 (Building Custom AI Skills) is next, where you'll package workflows like this into reusable slash commands.
